description: From medieval defenders to modern frontline soldiers — women's evolving role in British warfare.
content_html:
Women and War: A Changing Story

The role of women in British warfare has changed dramatically across the eras. In the medieval period, women were largely excluded from formal military roles but could be drawn into defence by circumstance. By the twentieth century, women served in auxiliary military organisations and on the home front. By the twenty-first century, women serve in combat roles alongside men. Tracing this change — and the continuities — reveals how attitudes to gender, citizenship and military service have shifted over 1,500 years.

Women in Medieval Warfare

Nicolaa de la Haye is one of the most striking examples of female military leadership in medieval England. She served as hereditary constable of Lincoln Castle and, in 1217 during the First Barons’ War, successfully defended the castle against rebel forces supporting the French prince Louis. King Henry III subsequently confirmed her position, recognising her military contribution. Nicolaa’s example shows that, while women were generally excluded from the feudal military system, high-ranking noblewomen with control of strategic fortifications could exercise genuine military authority.

More commonly, women in medieval England contributed to war effort indirectly — managing estates while husbands were on campaign, providing supplies and labour, and occasionally facing siege conditions alongside male garrison troops. Their role was essential but largely unrecorded and unrecognised by contemporary chronicles.

Key Fact

Nicolaa de la Haye was the female castellan of Lincoln Castle who successfully defended it during the First Barons’ War in 1217. Her case shows that, in exceptional circumstances, medieval women could exercise genuine military command — though this was rare and depended on social rank and access to fortifications rather than any formal recognition of female military service.

Women and British Armies, 1500–1900

In the early modern and Napoleonic periods, women who accompanied British armies served in supporting roles that were informally tolerated but rarely officially recognised. Camp followers provided cooking, laundry and nursing. Some women served as nurses at regimental level. Prostitution was widespread in and around military camps and was tacitly accepted as a reality of campaign life, though officially discouraged.

The Crimean War (1853–1856) produced two women whose contributions transformed the image of female nursing in warfare. Florence Nightingale reorganised the British military hospital at Scutari, introducing rigorous sanitation and supply management. The death rate among wounded soldiers at Scutari fell from approximately 40% to around 2% under her management — though historians continue to debate the precise figures and the relative contribution of different factors. Nightingale’s campaign for evidence-based healthcare reform continued long after the war.

Mary Seacole applied to join Nightingale’s nursing team and was rejected; she funded her own passage to the Crimea and established the “British Hotel” near the front, providing food, medical care and comfort to wounded soldiers. Her contribution was widely praised by soldiers at the time but was largely forgotten for most of the twentieth century until a major revival of her story from the 1980s onwards.

The Queen Alexandra’s Imperial Military Nursing Service (QAIMNS), established 1902, provided the professional framework for military nursing in the First World War. Over 10,000 women served as military nurses in the war, often working close to the front in casualty clearing stations. Nurses worked under shellfire, in extreme conditions, and often in close proximity to death and mass injury on a scale no previous generation had faced. Their service was formally recognised, though they did not receive full military status until later in the twentieth century.

Women on the Western Front: Flora Sandes and Dorothy Lawrence

A small number of women served in combat roles during the First World War. Flora Sandes began the war as a nurse in Serbia and, when the Serbian army faced collapse, continued fighting as a soldier. She was officially enlisted into the Serbian army, took part in combat, was wounded by a grenade in 1916, and was awarded the Order of Kara&dj;or&dj;e. Her case was exceptional: no other British woman served formally in a combat role in an Allied army during the First World War.

Dorothy Lawrence disguised herself as a male soldier and served on the Western Front as a sapper (combat engineer) in 1915 for ten days before her identity was discovered and she was discharged. Her case illustrates the social barrier that prevented women from serving in combat: her commanding officers were more concerned about the risk of embarrassment than about her demonstrated ability to serve.

Women in the Second World War

The Second World War saw the largest mobilisation of British women in history. The Auxiliary Territorial Service (ATS), Women’s Royal Naval Service (WRNS — informally “WRENs”) and Women’s Auxiliary Air Force (WAAF) collectively employed hundreds of thousands of women in support roles: operating radar and anti-aircraft batteries, working as drivers and mechanics, coding and communications work, and intelligence analysis. Women in ATS anti-aircraft units operated the targeting instruments — though they were not permitted to actually fire the guns until late in the war.

The Women’s Land Army mobilised approximately 80,000 women to work on farms by 1944, helping to maintain food production during the period when German U-boats threatened Britain’s supply lines. Their contribution was essential to home front survival.

Key Fact

The ATS, WRENs and WAAF employed hundreds of thousands of women in the Second World War in roles including radar operation, driving and logistics, code-breaking and intelligence. Women in the ATS operated anti-aircraft targeting instruments. The Women’s Land Army employed approximately 80,000 women on farms by 1944. These organisations represented the most systematic use of women in British military history to that point.

Women in the British armed forces were formally excluded from close-combat roles until 2016, when the ban was lifted. From January 2016, all military roles — including the infantry and special forces selection — became open to women. Sarah Bushbye, a corporal in the Royal Military Police, was cited in the spec as an example of women serving in frontline roles in recent operations. The change from total exclusion from the medieval military structure to full legal eligibility for any role represents one of the most significant social changes in the history of British warfare.
exam_tip_html: Questions about women in war often link to the theme of change and continuity. Make sure you can demonstrate change across all three eras: medieval (exceptional women like Nicolaa de la Haye, generally excluded), nineteenth–early twentieth century (nursing roles expanding; Flora Sandes exceptional), and modern (full integration into all roles by 2016). Don’t just describe what women did — explain what their contributions show about changing social attitudes and the extent to which change was genuinely continuous or came in sudden steps. Specific named examples (Florence Nightingale, Mary Seacole, Flora Sandes, Dorothy Lawrence) are essential for top-band answers.
conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Women were generally excluded from medieval military roles, though exceptional noblewomen like Nicolaa de la Haye (Lincoln, 1217) could exercise military command. Nursing roles expanded from the Crimean War (Florence Nightingale, Mary Seacole, 1854–56) into the First World War (QAIMNS) and Second World War (ATS, WRENs, WAAF).
  • Flora Sandes served as a soldier in the Serbian army in the First World War; Dorothy Lawrence disguised herself to serve on the Western Front in 1915 but was discovered and discharged, illustrating the social barriers of the era.
  • From 2016, all British military roles — including infantry and special forces — became open to women, completing a transformation that began with the Crimean War nursing reforms.

practice_questions.text: Describe one feature of Florence Nightingale's contribution to nursing in the Crimean War.
practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 2 marks:
• Florence Nightingale reorganised the military hospital at Scutari [1], introducing rigorous sanitation that dramatically reduced the death rate among wounded soldiers [1].
• She used statistical evidence to campaign for healthcare reform [1+1].

practice_questions.text: Describe two features of women's roles in the Second World War.
practice_questions.marks:
Award 2 marks per feature:
• Feature 1: Women in the ATS, WRENs and WAAF performed support roles including radar operation, driving, communications and intelligence [1], releasing men for frontline combat duties [1].
• Feature 2: The Women’s Land Army employed approximately 80,000 women on farms by 1944 [1], maintaining food production while German U-boats threatened supply lines [1].

practice_questions.text: Explain one reason why the role of women in British warfare changed significantly during the First World War.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Explains that the scale of casualties and the demands of industrial warfare created a need for large numbers of support workers; the QAIMNS and other organisations were created or expanded to fill gaps left by men serving at the front. The contribution of women on the home front and in support roles changed public and official attitudes, setting the stage for expanded roles in the Second World War.
Secure: Clear explanation with relevant evidence.
Developing: Identifies a cause with limited development.
Emerging: Simple statement.

practice_questions.text: Explain the significance of Flora Sandes in the context of women's roles in warfare.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Explains her significance at the time (the only British woman to serve formally as a soldier in an Allied army in the First World War; wounded in action and decorated) and her broader significance as evidence that women were capable of frontline service when given the opportunity, even when contemporary Britain maintained a clear prohibition. Analyses what her example shows about the gap between capability and social/institutional permission.
Secure: Explains significance with evidence.
Developing: Describes Flora Sandes with limited analysis.
Emerging: Simple statement.

practice_questions.text: How significant was the Second World War in changing the role of women in British warfare?
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Argues significance at the time (hundreds of thousands of women formally mobilised; ATS, WRENs, WAAF; Women’s Land Army) and over time (established the principle of systematic female military contribution; set precedents for later equality measures; the 2016 lifting of the frontline ban was the logical endpoint). Reaches a substantiated conclusion on significance compared to the Crimean War changes.
Secure: Explains significance with two horizons and relevant evidence.
Developing: One horizon, limited analysis.
Emerging: Describes the Second World War role without evaluating significance.

practice_questions.text: How far did the role of women in British warfare change between c.500 and the present day?
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Traces change across medieval (Nicolaa de la Haye exceptional; general exclusion), nineteenth century (Nightingale, Seacole — nursing beginning formal recognition), First World War (QAIMNS; Flora Sandes exceptional; Dorothy Lawrence excluded), Second World War (ATS/WRENs/WAAF systematic mobilisation), modern (2016 all roles open). Identifies continuity (nursing/support roles persistent; change in combat roles came slowly and against resistance). Weighs change against continuity; reaches a substantiated overall judgement.
Secure: Covers three periods with evidence and analysis.
Developing: Two periods, limited analysis.
Emerging: One period, no analytical framework.

options: A First World War nurse who worked at Scutari

The female castellan of Lincoln Castle who defended it in 1217
A British woman who served as a soldier with the Serbian army

flashcard_questions.a: The female castellan of Lincoln Castle who successfully defended it during the First Barons' War in 1217.

flashcard_questions.q: What hospital did Florence Nightingale reorganise in the Crimean War?
flashcard_questions.a: The British military hospital at Scutari.

flashcard_questions.q: What was Mary Seacole's contribution in the Crimean War?
flashcard_questions.a: She funded her own passage and ran the 'British Hotel' near Balaclava, providing care and supplies to wounded soldiers.
Queen Alexandra's Imperial Military Nursing Service — the professional military nursing service that expanded greatly in the First World War.

flashcard_questions.q: What is Flora Sandes known for in the First World War?
flashcard_questions.a: The only British woman to serve formally as a soldier in an Allied army, rising to sergeant major in the Serbian army.

flashcard_questions.q: What did Dorothy Lawrence do in 1915?
flashcard_questions.a: She disguised herself as a male soldier and served on the Western Front as a sapper for ten days before being discovered.

flashcard_questions.q: What were the three main women's military organisations in the Second World War?
flashcard_questions.a: ATS (Auxiliary Territorial Service), WRENs (Women's Royal Naval Service), WAAF (Women's Auxiliary Air Force).

When was the ban on women in British frontline combat roles lifted?

flashcard_questions.a: That high-ranking noblewomen could exercise genuine military command in exceptional circumstances, though this was rare.

glossary_terms.definition: A noblewoman who governed Lincolnshire as Sheriff and castellan, renowned for defending Lincoln Castle during the First Barons' War in 1217.
A pioneering nurse (1820–1910) who organised hospital care at Scutari during the Crimean War, dramatically reducing death rates through improved sanitation.
A Jamaican-born nurse (1805–1881) who travelled to the Crimea at her own expense and provided care closer to the front lines, running the 'British Hotel' near Balaclava.
Medical facilities positioned close to the front lines, designed to stabilise wounded soldiers before transfer to base hospitals.
A British woman (1876–1956) who served as a soldier with the Serbian army during the First World War, rising to the rank of sergeant major and being wounded in action in 1916.
A British organisation (1939–1950) that recruited and organised women for agricultural work to replace the men who had left for military service.
